sections.html:
• Scientific name: Euphyllia glabrescens (described in 1821 by Adelbert von Chamisso and Karl Wilhelm Eysenhardt)
  • Other names: Pom Pom Coral, Cornet Coral, Trumpet Coral
  • Type: large polyp stony (LPS) coral
  • Minimum tank size: 20 gallons (80 litres)
  • Keeping: moderate; propagation: easy
  • Lighting: moderate to high; water flow: moderate
  • Temperature: 23–28°C; salinity: SG 1.023–1.025; pH 8.1–8.4; KH 8–12; nitrate below 20 ppm
  • Feeding: photosynthetic (with supplemental feeding)
  • Tank placement: bottom to middle; growth rate: slow to moderate
  • Toxicity: yes; temper: aggressive; not invasive
  • Colours: red, purple, grey, yellow, blue, green, brown, pink, orange and others

Corals of the Euphyllia genus are widely available and Torch corals are no exception. They are commonly sold in pet stores and can also be sourced online from reputable reefers. Price depends mainly on size, colour and rarity; the Golden Torch is the most expensive.
A widely distributed coral species common to the Indo-Pacific reef regions: Fiji, Solomon Islands, the Great Barrier Reef, Australia and Asia, and rare in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.

Torch corals inhabit a wide range of reef environments. Their colonies are usually found on reef slopes in fairly deep, turbid waters down to a depth of 40 m.

Torch coral is a large polyp stony (LPS) coral with a calcified skeletal base, forming phaceloid colonies (individual corallite tubes joined at the base). The corallites of Euphyllia glabrescens are 20–30 mm across and 15–30 mm apart. The corallite walls are thin and sharp-edged, and the polyps are long and fleshy and can retract completely into the skeleton. Sweeper tentacles can range from 2.5 to 20 cm. Septa are not exsert and columellae are absent. Colonial polyps are connected by the coenosarc, which lets them share nutrients.

The polyps have large tubular tentacles with round or knob-like tips. Tentacle colour varies: brown, grey-blue, grey-green, yellow, or purple/pink, with cream, green, pink or white tips. The golden torch is a rare and highly sought-after variety.

In aquariums, colonies usually reach about 12–25 cm, while in nature a colony can be up to 1 m. Torch corals do not grow very fast, but under optimal conditions they can live for dozens of years.

Torch corals should be kept apart from other corals and can grow quite large, so a 20 gallon (80 litre) tank is the minimum size. Larger tanks are even better, as they allow adequate spacing between corals and more stable water parameters.

Torch corals are not easy to take care of. It is challenging but not impossible, and very rewarding when all goes well.

Make partial water changes of 20–25% monthly, 10–15% every two weeks, or 5% weekly to maintain good water quality and replenish trace elements. Do not change more than 25% of the water at one time.

Inspect the corals regularly so that damage, infection or unusual changes in behaviour are detected promptly. Routine checks and a good water change schedule are key to managing water chemistry and keeping the corals healthy.

Temperature: 24–28°C. pH: 8.1–8.4. Hardness: 8–12 dKH.

Additional parameters to maintain consistently:

  • Calcium: 400–450 ppm (the major building block of LPS corals)
  • Magnesium: 1,250–1,350 ppm
  • Salinity/specific gravity: 1.023–1.025
  • Strontium: 8–10 ppm
  • Phosphate: below 0.05 ppm
  • Ammonia: 0 ppm
  • Nitrate: below 20 ppm (some reports say Torch corals dislike nitrate, which stresses and weakens them)

Lighting: Torch corals need moderate to high lighting for best growth, coloration and health. Too much light can cause bleaching. They enjoy diffused light and appreciate metal halides, but light from this source can be too intense if the coral is placed directly under it, and metal halides give off a lot of heat that may damage the polyps and cause rapid tissue necrosis. LED lighting of around 75–150 PAR is sufficient. Torch corals generally change colour depending on the lighting, whether white or blue.

Water flow: Flow should be moderate, not too weak or too strong, and good enough to keep detritus from settling on the coral. Strong flow can damage the coral or prevent the polyps from extending fully, so if a Torch coral will not open, check whether the flow is too strong. It also depends on the Torch coral type: in nature, purple-gold Torch corals are found at river mouths, with very strong flow and brackish water influence, where the sediments are different.

As with all LPS corals, Torch corals have a symbiotic relationship with zooxanthellae living in their tissue, which lets them obtain nutrients through photosynthesis. Although this is enough to survive, they benefit greatly from supplemental or manual feeding. Do not overfeed: overfeeding is one reason Torch corals may develop brown jelly infection.

They can be fed:

  • mysis shrimp
  • vitamin-enriched brine shrimp
  • krill
  • plankton
  • specialised pellet food
  • copepods
  • reef roids

It is best to spot feed by mixing the food with a little saltwater and squirting it directly onto the coral head with a turkey baster or pipette. Feeding several times a week results in increased growth, more polyp extension and puffier body tissue. Turn off the flow to make spot feeding easier. If fish and shrimp interfere with feeding, consider using a feeding cage unless you distract them with other food.

Torch corals are active throughout the day and frequently extend their tentacles to draw food into their mouth. They are sessile and generally aggressive, and compete with other corals for space in the reef tank. Leave plenty of space between torches and any other coral or tankmate. They possess cnidocytes, explosive cells containing a giant secretory organelle called a nematocyst, used to deliver a painful sting to competitors and nearby organisms. These stinging cells help the coral immobilise and capture prey and also serve as a defence against predators.

It is not advisable to keep them even with their closest relatives, Frogspawn (Euphyllia divisa) and Hammer corals (Euphyllia ancora and Euphyllia paraancora); Torch corals will reduce them to a bare skeleton in no time. Torches can, however, be kept with other Torch corals.

Warning: although Torch corals usually cannot penetrate human skin, always be careful when handling corals. Their slime coating can still cause skin irritation, so wear rubber gloves when touching them.

Torch corals reproduce both sexually and asexually. In the wild, they release mature gametes (eggs and sperm) into the water; fertilisation takes place and gives rise to coral larvae (planulae). Under the right conditions, the free-swimming planulae metamorphose into polyps that attach to the surface where they settle.

In asexual reproduction, mature polyps reproduce by budding. Smaller polyps form around the base and either stay connected to the colony or break off, depending on environmental conditions, to establish a new colony. Long strings coming out of a Torch coral are a sign that its heads are about to split.

Another means of propagation is fragging a healthy coral. This is simple but requires caution:

  • Make sure your hands are clean or wear gloves.
  • Take out the coral and irritate it slightly so that it retracts its tentacles.
  • Cut it: a Torch coral can be divided by cutting through the branching corallites (where the flesh is completely separated), 5–7 cm below the head, without damaging the flesh. This is easily done with a band saw.
  • Attach the new frags to a frag plug or live rock using cyanoacrylate gel before returning them to the tank. Soak a ceramic frag plug in water for a couple of minutes first to release trapped air bubbles. Treat new frags with an iodine solution (for example Lugol's solution) to prevent disease before attaching them to live rock.

Items you may need, depending on method: hammer and chisel, scissors, cyanoacrylate glue, containers, scalpel/razor blade, plug pebbles/coral frag disks, a coral propagation fragging kit.

Placement in the tank

Torch corals can be aggressive toward other coral species, except those of their own genus, so other corals should be spaced well away from them. Place them where they will be comfortable and avoid being blasted by strong currents or direct lighting; this may take trial and error until a good spot is found. They do best in the lower sections of the tank and can be placed directly on the substrate or fastened to live rock. A sand bed gives indirect diffused light and moderately turbulent flow, but sand can get trapped in the calcified base. Live rock is the better option, as it gives moderate currents and prevents damage to the delicate tissue.

Tankmates

Torch corals should be placed at least 15–20 cm from any other coral, as their stings can be lethal to some. In the absence of sea anemones, clownfish are known to host in Torch corals, but this is not good: clownfish may accidentally damage the coral and cause infections such as brown jelly. The same applies to hermit crabs, crabs and similar animals. Torch corals do not like to be disturbed.

Common problems

Brown jelly: characterised by a brown, jelly-like goo that floats on the coral's surface and can spread to the whole colony or other corals if untreated. Causes include poor water quality, tissue damage and overfeeding. Treatment: move the coral to a separate tank or container, brush and siphon off all visible traces of jelly, and frag off infected heads to reduce spread. Dip the coral in freshwater (15 ppt) or an iodine solution to eliminate the infection; broad-spectrum antibiotics are also effective. Afterwards, keep the coral in a quarantine tank until fully recovered before returning it to the main tank.

Flatworms: Torch corals tend to carry hitchhikers such as coral-eating flatworms, which hide very well, usually between the coral flesh and the skeletal stalk. Quarantine and disinfect corals before putting them in the display tank. Do not place corals in the main tank right after treatment, as eggs may remain; the treatment may need to be repeated a couple of weeks apart.

Mishandling: handle corals with great care, especially during fragging. The skeleton has shattered in several cases when fragged with bone cutters, which can injure the fleshy polyp area. A band saw allows safer, more precise cutting than bone cutters and shears.
